section_summary: This section opens with U.S. diplomatic reports from Lima recording J. Salvador Sanchez’s allegations that Japanese immigrants, naval officers, army officers, landowners, and merchants in Peru formed a covert military network intended to support a future attack on the United States and the Panama Canal. Embassy and State Department officials sought further information but repeatedly questioned Sanchez’s reliability, while related documents address Japanese and Chinese propaganda in Peru and reactions to the Lytton Report. The section concludes with the first fifty-four pages of a Spanish-language, pro-Japanese book explaining the Sino-Japanese conflict, Manchuria, Pacific geopolitics, and Japan’s modernization and expansion.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1508: Alleged Japanese military activities in Peru
subfiles.from: Fred Morris Dearing, American Ambassador at Lima
subfiles.about: Reports J. Salvador Sanchez’s allegations that Japanese officers and settlers in Peru were preparing properties, personnel, and mobilization plans for a future attack on American interests.
subfiles.summary: Sanchez claimed that Japan had infiltrated Peru with soldiers disguised as immigrants and could mobilize thousands of men at coastal ports, especially for an attack on the Panama Canal. He identified Teizo Nishi, Kurikawa, Matsuda, and Nakamura as alleged naval or army figures involved in buying strategically located properties and said he had seen Japanese mobilization maps. Dearing noted the resemblance to earlier unfounded Japanese scare stories but forwarded the account because Sanchez appeared sincere.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 292 requesting further reports on Japanese activities
subfiles.from: Francis White, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Fred Morris Dearing, American Ambassador at Lima
subfiles.about: Directs the Embassy to submit further information about Japanese activities in Peru because the Director of Naval Intelligence had expressed interest.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Dearing’s despatch No. 1508. It asks him to continue reporting any information on Japanese activities that comes to his attention.

subfiles.title: File-number control slip
subfiles.about: Records an OCR-obscured decimal-file control number associated with the preceding correspondence.
subfiles.summary: The page contains only a file-number notation. It provides no substantive narrative or correspondence.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Chinese and Japanese propaganda in Peru
subfiles.about: Cross-references a Callao-Lima report by Burdett concerning propaganda pamphlets issued by Chinese and Japanese cultural societies.
subfiles.summary: The sheet directs readers to another file for a consular report on pamphlets concerning the Sino-Japanese conflict. It identifies the material as propaganda intended to influence opinion in Peru.

subfiles.title: Chinese and Japanese Propaganda in Peru
subfiles.from: William C. Burdett, American Consul General, Callao-Lima
subfiles.about: Forwards Chinese and Japanese cultural-society pamphlets intended to influence Peruvian public opinion.
subfiles.summary: Burdett reports the existence of competing Chinese and Japanese propaganda in Peru. He encloses one pamphlet issued by each nationality’s cultural society for the Department’s examination.

subfiles.title: Latin-American Affairs handwritten assessment of Sanchez’s statements
subfiles.about: Characterizes the allegations under review as fantastic and questions whether further circulation or action would be prudent.
subfiles.summary: The writer regards the statements as highly implausible. The note warns that pursuing them could mislead friendly governments or make American diplomats appear credulous, unless Far Eastern Affairs specifically wants action.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs comment on the Lima report
subfiles.about: Expresses doubt about Sanchez’s reported statements and leaves any action requested by the despatch to the Latin-American division.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs states that Sanchez’s claims in the attached Lima material do not sound convincing. It presumes that Latin-American Affairs will handle any action called for by the despatch’s final paragraph.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1709 forwarding further Sanchez information
subfiles.from: Fred Morris Dearing, American Ambassador at Lima
subfiles.about: Forwards Ackerson’s memorandum of an April 11 conversation with Sanchez and requests intelligence that might help verify or disprove the allegations.
subfiles.summary: Dearing says the Embassy cannot judge the trustworthiness of Sanchez or Gildred and has not yet verified the Japanese names and addresses provided. He proposes checking the claims locally and asks whether Navy intelligence can supply corroborating facts or statistics. The enclosed memorandum is identified as having been prepared by Ackerson.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with Sanchez and Gildred
subfiles.about: Records Sanchez’s expanded allegations of bribed immigration, Japanese military colonies, plans against the Panama Canal, worldwide war preparations, propaganda, and novel weapons.
subfiles.summary: Sanchez alleged that Japanese agents bribed officials to admit immigrants who were then settled on haciendas purchased by army officers, forming nuclei for a military force. He described supposed plans to disable the Panama Canal, restore Panama to Colombia, encourage debtor countries and colonies to revolt, seize the Philippines, and weaken Britain through propaganda in India. He also repeated claims about Japanese military superiority, gas protection, and a freezing bomb, while Ackerson noted that preliminary statistics instead showed more Japanese leaving Peru than entering it. The memorandum lists Kurikawa, Luis Zoppu, and Nakamura with addresses for possible checking.

subfiles.title: Division of Latin-American Affairs divider
subfiles.about: Marks an internal division or routing point in the file.
subfiles.summary: The page bears only the heading of the Division of Latin-American Affairs. It contains no substantive text.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs assessment of Despatch No. 2250
subfiles.about: Evaluates Sanchez’s latest allegations, explaining Japanese immigration institutions and finding no support for his reading of the Lima Nipo newspaper.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum argues that Sanchez mistook ordinary Japanese immigration officials and ex-service community leaders for secret War Office agents. Departmental examination of the October 3–4 Lima Nipo issues found no report that Japan’s military demanded war with America; the articles merely described familiar Japanese reactions to the Lytton Report. The writer suggests that Sanchez’s Japanese acquaintances may have been teasing him, although their bellicose attitudes were considered noteworthy.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2250: Further information from Sanchez
subfiles.from: Garret G. Ackerson Jr., for the American Ambassador at Lima
subfiles.about: Forwards Sanchez’s latest memorandum, Lima Nipo issues, a Spanish-language book, and the personal cards of Teizo Nishi and M. Kurikawa.
subfiles.summary: Sanchez again approached the Embassy with claims about Japanese preparations for war against the United States. Ackerson forwarded an excerpt of his memorandum, two issues of Lima Nipo, the book ¿Qué quiere el Japón? ¿Qué quiere la China?, and cards identifying Nishi as a Japanese naval officer and Kurikawa as his associate. The Embassy again declined to vouch for Sanchez’s accuracy but sent the material so the Department could compare it with wider intelligence sources.

subfiles.title: Translated excerpt from Sanchez’s memorandum
subfiles.about: Relates alleged Japanese reactions to the Lytton Report, expectations of imminent war with the United States, and Nishi and Kurikawa’s supposed 1918 land mission.
subfiles.summary: Sanchez reports being told that the October 3–4 Lima Nipo issues showed the Japanese armed services demanding war with the United States and the government seeking explanations over the Lytton Report. He repeats claims that Japanese settlers and officers in Hawaii and the Philippines awaited arms and orders, that Japan planned to foment revolutions in American Pacific possessions, and that the American fleet would be defeated. He also describes a marked passage in El drama del Extremo Oriente and states that Nishi and Kurikawa told him in 1918 that they were acquiring land for discharged Japanese soldiers, including settlers previously placed in Brazil.

subfiles.title: El drama del Extremo Oriente: ¿Qué quiere el Japón? ¿Qué quiere la China?
subfiles.from: J. C. Balet; Spanish edition credited to O. Fritz, with a preface by Georges Leygues
subfiles.about: Presents a pro-Japanese interpretation of Pacific geopolitics, the Sino-Japanese conflict, Manchuria, and Japan’s modernization and territorial expansion.
subfiles.summary: The title page and prefatory material portray Balet as an experienced observer of China, Japan, Korea, Manchuria, and Russia and explicitly argue that treaty violations by China caused the current conflict. Chapter One surveys the principal Pacific powers, recounts Western incursions into China and Japan, and presents Japanese expansion as a defensive response to Russian, Chinese, British, and American pressure. Chapter Two describes Manchurian history, geography, resources, migration, Korean settlement, and banditry while justifying Japanese intervention and economic activity. Chapter Three begins a laudatory account of Japan’s national unification, modernization, treaty revision, wars with China and Russia, annexation of Korea, and alignment with Britain.
